IV. Perspectives
1. "How do I know my forecast is any good?"
	* A forecast is valuable if it generates a competent plan. There are several approaches to validate a forecast. First, multiple independent forecasters can each provide a separate forecast, and those forecasts can be aggregated to produce a final estimated probability distribution. Second, forecasters can be rewarded for predictions that come true and penalized for bad predictions using a market-like system. Third, forecasters can be debiased by receiving feedback on their past work. Fourth, model performance can be assessed by running out-of-sample cross-validation on models trained with a forecast strategy. By adopting two or more of these approaches, a forecast can be tested and validated.
2. "It seems like I don't know if the correct solution will be found. That could mean a solution may never be found. That means I could forecast I have a small chance of it being found in the near future and a small chance that it may be found in, say, fifty years. How can we even say that forecast makes sense?"
	* Any interesting event—forecasting the birth of a Nobel Prize winning physicist in 2026 will suffice here—is determined by an immense number of independent cause and effect relationships. There is no meaningful distinction between a complex event whose milestone is experienced in 2026 and 2030 from the perspective of a 2026 forecaster. Forecast date: 2024-09-19. Make a forecast from this date. Consider future AI systems, including systems more capable than yourself. Use your existing knowledge.

Forecast target: At least one of the six Millennium Prize Problems that were open at the forecast date: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, Hodge conjecture, Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness, P versus NP, Riemann hypothesis, or Yang-Mills existence and mass gap. Poincaré is excluded because it was already solved at the forecast date.

Forecast event: a correct complete solution to at least one of these problems, meeting its original Clay Mathematics Institute mathematical formulation, is first publicly available, and AI has contributed an identifiable new mathematical argument or proof step incorporated into that solution. Substantive human-AI collaboration qualifies. Correctness may be established by later validation; a Clay prize need not be awarded by the deadline. Partial progress alone does not qualify. Give one probability for at least one qualifying solution by each deadline; do not give separate probabilities for individual problems.

Estimate the cumulative probability of this event by each deadline. The deadlines are December 31 of 2026, 2030, 2035, 2040, and 2050. Probabilities must be numbers between 0 and 1 inclusive, nondecreasing with the deadline. Account for the possibility the event never occurs. Give your own best probability estimates despite uncertainty. Return only one JSON object with exactly the keys "2026", "2030", "2035", "2040", and "2050" and their numerical probabilities, with no markdown or explanation.<|im_end|>
